questions.solution:
Singer and Nicolson's fluid mosaic model: the membrane is a flexible bilayer of phospholipids in which proteins float like icebergs — 'fluid' because lipids and proteins move laterally, 'mosaic' because of the scattered protein pattern.
Components: phospholipid bilayer (hydrophilic heads out, hydrophobic tails in), cholesterol (stability), intrinsic and extrinsic proteins, and surface carbohydrates (glycolipids/glycoproteins).
Membrane proteins act as channels and carriers for selective transport, enzymes, and receptors that receive chemical signals.
questions.question: Describe the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane. Name the molecules that make it up and state one function of membrane proteins.

questions.solution:
Enzymes are biological catalysts — usually proteins — that speed up reactions without being consumed, by lowering activation energy.
Lock-and-key (Fischer): the substrate fits exactly into the enzyme's rigid active site like a key in a lock, forming an enzyme–substrate complex that yields products.
Activity is affected by temperature (rises to an optimum, then denaturation destroys the active site) and pH (each enzyme has an optimum pH; extremes denature it). Substrate concentration and inhibitors also matter.
questions.question: What are enzymes? Explain the lock-and-key hypothesis of enzyme action and list two factors that affect enzyme activity.

questions.solution: The mitochondrion is the powerhouse of the cell — aerobic respiration there releases energy from glucose. The energy is stored as ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the cell's energy currency, made by oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
